KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong/long duration Nor'easter will bring strong to 
damaging wind gusts, coastal flooding/beach erosion, and periods of 
heavy rain  late Fri through the weekend. Power outages are a 
concern  particularly along the coast with fully leafed trees.  

An early season/long duration Nor'easter will bring a variety of 
impactful weather to southern New England later Fri right through 
the weekend. While there remains some uncertainty on the exact track 
and where the worst of the impacts are felt...confidence is 
relatively high that this will be an impactful storm for our region. 

There are several moving parts that our ideal for a strong early 
season Nor'easter. The high pressure over Quebec and the offshore 
low pressure system are both indicated to be outside the EPS/GEFS 
models climatology. This will result in a strong persistent NE 
gradient of wind beginning Fri and continuing into Sunday. While 
there remain track differences...the low pressure system initially 
backs westward to a position somewhere south of Long Island before 
eventually lifting NE and gradually weakening through early next 
week. This is the reason that this storm will be of such long 
duration. The easterly LLJ is also shown to be outside the models 
climatology. This will not only result in the forcing for bands of 
rain moving across the region...But several impacts that we will 
break down below.

1) Strong to Damaging Wind Gusts... 

The biggest concern with the strong NE winds are that they will be 
of both long duration and also coupled with heavy rain/fully leafed 
trees. This will exacerbate the risk for tree damage and power 
outages than if this same storm were occurring a few months later. 
The strongest of the winds will be along the coast...where we expect 
NE wind gust of 45 to 60 mph. It is also possible a few spots see 
winds reach 65-70 mph across the Islands...but that will be 
dependent on the track. Regardless...whether or not places hit 
specific high wind criteria is less important that the long duration 
combined with the fully leafed trees. Given that factor...we opted 
to go with High Wind Warnings along the coast. Further inland...we 
are expecting NE wind gusts of 30 to 45 mph but a few gusts near 50 
mph are possible in heavier bands of rain. Again...given the fully 
leafed trees combined with long duration of the event opted to issue 
a Wind Advisory. The wind and tree damage/power outage risk will be 
the biggest impact for most people. 

2) Beach Erosion/Coastal Flooding...

The other big issue with this storm will be the expected beach 
erosion/coastal flooding issues over multiple high tide cycles. 
While this will not be a storm under-going rapid bombogenesis...but 
the persistence of these strong NE winds and high seas offshore are 
concerning. A storm surge on the order of 1 to 2 feet and perhaps 
briefly near 2.5 feet are expected late Fri right through the 
weekend along east face ocean exposed beaches. We extended the 
Coastal Flood Watch in these locations through Sunday. This along 
with 15 to 25 foot seas offshore will result in pockets of minor 
coastal flooding/beach erosion during each high tide cycle late Fri 
through the weekend and a few pockets of low end moderate coastal 
flooding are also possible. Astronomical high tides are increasing 
through the weekend...so even as winds eventually start to slowly 
diminish these issues will be a concern. Given this event will 
impact multiple high tide cycles...the water may struggle to drain 
out after each high tide. Heavy rainfall may also exacerbate these 
issues a well. Overall...the biggest impact from this system may be 
in regards to beach erosion given such a long duration event. 

While NE winds will result in less coastal flood impacts on the 
south coast...high seas just offshore and swell may result in some 
splashover/minor coastal flooding in these locations as well. This 
is something we will need to watch.

3) Heavy Rain and Timing...

Lastly...periods of heavy rain will be impacting the region at times 
later Fri into the weekend. This is one area where there remains 
some significant differences on how quickly the rain shield 
overspreads the region from southeast to the northwest. The GFS/RGEM 
are on the faster side with rain ovespreading most of the region 
later Fri into Fri night. Meanwhile...the ECMWF/NAM struggle to 
bring steady rain into much of the interior until Sat. We blended 
the differences for now...but once the rain arrives will basically 
continue through the weekend and even into Mon. Rainfall totals of 1-
4" are possible with the highest amounts most likely near the coast. 
We opted not to issue a Flood Watch given some of the model guidance 
takes the heaviest rain south of our region and given the fact that 
its over a long duration.
